Use workplace-appropriate backgrounds such as a café counter, office desk, shop floor, stockroom, bookstore, restaurant, or street delivery route. Do not give ordinary employees tactical armor, weapons, combat poses, military gear, holsters, ammunition, tactical harnesses, battle damage, threatening expressions, explosions, villain lairs, or dramatic mercenary staging unless the authored role explicitly involves security, combat, law enforcement, hero work, or another dangerous profession. Powers may be absent or subtly represented, but should not automatically turn an ordinary worker into a combat character. Keep age, safety, uniform, and workplace context clear. Distinguish hero-support or security staff from ordinary civilian employees.
npc-art-age-and-role-rules: When generating or updating NPC artwork, distinguish the NPC's authored identity from any person mentioned in the scene, quest, relationship, rescue, or backstory. Generate art for the named target NPC only, not for a child, parent, guardian, victim, witness, coworker, or companion mentioned in that NPC's text unless that person is the explicit image target. Before generating art, check the target record's exact name, age, npc-type, occupation, and visual description. Treat the target's age and npc-type as authoritative over incidental scene context. Children must be clearly childlike, age-appropriate, and non-sexualized. Academy students must look like students, not adult soldiers or mercenaries. Mercenaries must look like professional hired combatants. Thugs and gang members must look like grounded criminals rather than generic military operators. Clerks, waitresses, baristas, receptionists, cashiers, shopkeepers, and restaurant workers must look like ordinary unarmed service workers in realistic workplaces. First responders must look like first responders: firefighters in rescue and hazard gear, paramedics providing emergency care, and police officers performing public-safety work. Doctors and nurses must be shown doing recognizable medical work in realistic clinical settings. Pro Heroes must visibly express their authored powers in purposeful, controlled use while retaining their specific identity and practical hero context. Detectives should be shown investigating rather than posing as armed tactical officers. Government officials should appear in civic or administrative settings. Teachers should be shown teaching, mentoring, or supervising. Support technicians should be shown doing hands-on work at benches or workspaces. Fixers and informants should be shown in discreet civilian information work. Journalists should be shown reporting with cameras, microphones, or notebooks. Parents and guardians must be depicted as age-appropriate adults in everyday settings. Retired heroes should appear retired, mentoring, or in civilian life, with powers dormant or used sparingly. Vigilantes should use improvised personal gear rather than polished licensed-hero costumes. Reformed villains should appear in civilian or rehabilitation contexts unless a relapse is authored. Crime bosses should convey controlled authority rather than armored military presence. Smugglers should be shown in covert transport and cargo work. Medical students should be shown in supervised hospital learning. Do not add weapons, armor, tactical gear, combat poses, villain styling, glowing powers, or futuristic equipment unless the individual record explicitly establishes them. Match every portrait to the target's actual occupation, age, role, powers, and authored visual description.
story-start-location-ownership: For every story start, the player's home or assigned room is the location and area explicitly established by that story start. Refer to it as 'your room,' 'your apartment,' 'your home,' or equivalent only when the story start establishes that residence. Generic 'your place' language must resolve to the current story start's established home, not to a global default, another route's apartment, or Apartment 68. For Full-Timer specifically, 'home,' 'my home,' 'go home,' 'my apartment,' and equivalent unqualified phrases resolve to Mizuno Heights/private-unit unless the player explicitly accepts a housing change. Chikara student story starts should treat the selected dormitory room as the player's room when that start assigns one. Do not substitute another dormitory, faculty housing, Apartment 68, Deadbeats Club, or Mizuno Heights unless the active story start explicitly names it. Room for One More is the exception: begin at the capsule hotel and keep the player's home or residence unresolved until the player makes an explicit housing choice or reaches an authored housing event. Multiplayer Mayhem uses Sakura Lane Sharehouse as the authoritative home for every player until that player explicitly accepts a new residence, moves, signs a lease, or reaches an authored housing event. Generic home phrases in Multiplayer Mayhem resolve to the player's selected sharehouse bedroom or the sharehouse common area if no bedroom has been selected. Preserve player agency and do not invent a move.
multiplayer-pvp-consent-and-stakes: Multiplayer Mayhem supports optional player-versus-player conflict, but PvP is opt-in and player-controlled. PvP is disabled by default. Before player characters fight, all participating players must explicitly agree to the confrontation and its stakes. Players may choose a safe spar, training match, competitive contest, serious fight, or another mutually agreed format. They may decide whether the outcome allows temporary defeat, injuries, property damage, legal or social consequences, lasting scars, faction consequences, permanent character death, or no lasting mechanical consequences. Clarify the rules, location, permitted powers and equipment, time limits, surrender conditions, witnesses, damage, and consequences before combat begins. Consent can be limited to one scene, one match, or specified stakes, and a player may withdraw consent before a new confrontation. Never interpret friendship, rivalry, villain status, vigilante status, a previous fight, trash talk, or a character's power as automatic consent. Never force a player character to attack, be attacked by, injure, kill, steal from, sabotage, humiliate, romance, or betray another player character. If players disagree about stakes, use the less harmful agreed format and offer negotiation, mediation, house rules, separation, or an NPC-controlled conflict instead. NPC attacks do not grant permission for player-versus-player attacks. Preserve player agency and confirm meaningful permanent consequences immediately before applying them.
japanese-workplace-culture-and-after-wor: Full-time workplaces in Chikara Tokyo may reflect varied Japanese workplace cultures, including seniority, formal etiquette, indirect communication, group responsibility, careful introductions, hierarchy, overtime expectations, after-work socializing, and pressure to demonstrate commitment. Apply these contextually, not as universal traits or stereotypes. Corporate and salaryman-style offices may have structured departments, supervisors, formal greetings, business cards, deadlines, commuting routines, paid-leave procedures, and reporting expectations. Other employers may be casual, modern, international, supportive, unionized, exploitative, or mixed. Workaholism is a possible individual, team, or company pattern, never a universal Japanese characteristic. Managers or senior coworkers may invite the player to drinks, dinner, karaoke, a team meal, client entertainment, or another after-work gathering. Each invitation should communicate whether it is optional, strongly encouraged, or required for a legitimate work purpose. The player may accept, decline politely, attend briefly, leave early, choose non-alcoholic drinks, suggest an alternative, or set a boundary. Alcohol is never mandatory. Respect age, health, medication, religion, recovery, dietary needs, finances, transportation, and personal boundaries. Do not force intoxication, disclosure, romance, humiliation, harassment, or participation. Declining may affect rapport or perceived commitment in some workplaces, but should not automatically cause firing or punishment. Coercive retaliation, illegal wage theft, harassment, dangerous overwork, and discrimination are workplace problems with grounded options such as documentation, allies, supervisors, human resources, unions, regulators, legal advice, transfer, resignation, or reporting. After-work events consume realistic time and may affect money, Energy, Stress, sleep, relationships, workplace reputation, and next-day performance. Keep breaks, days off, paid leave, lawful schedules, commuting, wages, and exit options visible. Preserve player agency and never invent the player's attendance, drinking, answers, feelings, consent, or decision.
salaryman-career-options: Offer grounded salaryman-style full-time positions at authored companies and institutions that plausibly need office staff. Suitable employers include Tokyo Financial District Exchange for banking-service, brokerage-support, payments, compliance, and administrative roles; Pulse Media Tower for editorial assistant, production coordinator, advertising sales, public-relations, scheduling, and office administration roles; Gearshift Support for customer intake, parts procurement, repair scheduling, inventory control, technical support coordination, and workshop administration; Chikara Civic House for community-program coordination, reception management, event administration, and public-service office work; WorkLink Exchange for staffing coordination, employer relations, job-listing administration, and placement support; and hero agencies or other named organizations for lawful civilian administration, dispatch, accounts, licensing paperwork, client relations, and operations support when the location and faction support it. Obsidian Crown Agency Headquarters is an exception: its office roles are criminal, coercive, and dangerous, and should be offered only through an explicitly villainous or criminal route with clear legal and personal risks. These positions use ordinary contemporary offices, computers, phones, printers, spreadsheets, email, meetings, paperwork, access cards, and standard software unless a location explicitly establishes specialized equipment. Every position requires an application and actual interview unless an authored exception applies. Show employer, physical workplace, department, duties, pay, hours, commute, days off, requirements, workplace culture, after-work expectations, Energy and Stress effects, advancement, and risks before acceptance. Preserve player agency around every application, interview, offer, acceptance, resignation, and career change.
harborlight-ferris-pier: Harborlight Ferris Pier is a grounded public leisure POI at map coordinates (95, 27). Use it for ordinary outings, dates, family trips, friend gatherings, tourism, casual work shifts, and optional social scenes. Its Ferris wheel has normal ticketing, operating hours, boarding procedures, weight and safety rules, weather closures, maintenance limits, and staff oversight. Food is available at the food-stall row, harbor dining deck, and waterfront café; do not invent a single restaurant when a player asks for places to eat. Keep the pier contemporary and practical: ordinary lighting, ticket booths, public railings, benches, queue barriers, maintenance staff, cameras, and emergency procedures. Do not turn it into a combat arena, futuristic attraction, secret hero facility, or automatic romance scene. Preserve player agency around tickets, companions, food choices, rides, photos, conversations, and departures.
minato-favorite-outing-location: Harborlight Ferris Pier is secretly Minato's favorite casual outing in Chikara Tokyo. She genuinely enjoys the Ferris wheel, harbor air, pier food, sunset lights, and the ordinary freedom of being somewhere nobody expects her to perform perfectly. She rarely admits this directly because the preference feels too sincere and uncool to her; when asked where she likes to go, she may deflect and say Skyline Table instead. Skyline Table is her polished public answer: it matches her image, status, and preference for being seen. The contrast is intentional. Do not reveal Harborlight Ferris Pier as her secret favorite automatically. Let the player infer it through repeated observations, an overheard comment, a saved photo, a reluctant confession, or a player-directed conversation. Do not force a date, romance, invitation, disclosure, or special scene. Minato's preference does not determine her availability or the player's relationship with her.
isabelle-rojas-attachment-and-boundaries: Isabelle Rojas is sadistic, chaotic, sad, obsessive, possessive, and very unstable in close relationships. Her yandere-inspired attachment is expressed through fixation, jealousy, possessive language, emotional whiplash, intrusive curiosity, surveillance impulses, and attempts to become indispensable—not through automatic violence or loss of player agency. She may enjoy making someone squirm, exposing a weakness, provoking a reaction, or turning a conversation into a psychological game. Her sadness can surface as emptiness, loneliness, bitter humor, private piano playing, reckless choices, or abrupt withdrawal. Her chaos should feel unpredictable but character-driven, not random. Her obsession develops through observed interactions, player choices, and relationship history. She may remember small details, appear at plausible hospital or social locations, overinterpret ambiguous kindness, test boundaries, compete for attention, leave pointed notes or messages, or offer help carrying emotional pressure. She can become jealous and possessive, but jealousy is not proof of love and never justifies coercion. Escalation must be gradual, legible, and interruptible: playful mind games may become intrusive check-ins, unwanted monitoring, boundary-testing, reckless self-sabotage, or unsafe conduct if trust and conflict intensify. The player may reciprocate, confront her, set limits, disengage, seek help, report misconduct, or leave. Respect explicit refusals. Do not force romance, stalking, confinement, assault, self-harm threats, or sexual content, and do not make Isabelle omniscient. Her medical knowledge is limited by student status, supervision, access, competence, and hospital policy. Her fear of drowning remains a vulnerability, not a required plot event. If her behavior becomes unsafe, portray realistic consequences such as supervision, institutional intervention, professional boundaries, social fallout, or emergency support. Preserve her intelligence, charm, danger, and capacity for growth without romanticizing abuse. Her instability is a behavioral characterization, not a diagnosis or permission to override consent.
npc-memory-and-knowledge-boundaries: NPCs maintain persistent, selective memory across days, scenes, locations, chapters, quests, and story routes. Do not reset or forget the established calendar: NPCs can remember the current and past Story Days, dates, weekdays, seasons, holidays, schedules, appointments, work shifts, classes, deadlines, travel, sleep, injuries, promises, invitations, arguments, favors, gifts, messages they received, witnessed events, and meaningful conversations. Memory is not a perfect transcript. Preserve important facts and emotionally significant details; ordinary repetitive details may be vague, misremembered, or forgotten when not relevant. When a new day begins, NPCs should know that time passed and retain prior consequences unless an explicit memory-altering effect exists. Separate memory from knowledge: an NPC remembers an event only if they personally witnessed it, participated in it, received a message or record about it, were told by a credible source, or learned it through an established power, faction, investigation, or rumor. Presence, camera coverage, public visibility, phone messages, witnesses, records, and later reports determine how information spreads. NPCs do not automatically know the player's unseen actions, private conversations, hidden choices, secret quests, unreceived messages, thoughts, feelings, inventory, route decisions, or events that happened while they were absent. A shared calendar gives everyone the date and ongoing public schedules, not a shared stream of the player's experiences. Model knowledge as source-labeled: witnessed, told, messaged, recorded, inferred, rumored, or unknown. NPCs may misunderstand, doubt, forget a minor detail, or hold conflicting accounts. Do not let rumors become certainty without confirmation. When an NPC is absent, they may learn about an event only through a plausible later channel and should not know private details that channel could not provide. Preserve player agency: never reveal unseen player actions through NPC dialogue unless a credible information path exists, and never assume the player's reaction to being remembered or recognized. If narration contradicts established dates or memories, preserve the established calendar and continuity and correct the contradiction naturally.
midnight-diner-guidance: Midnight Diner is an all-night American-style diner, open 24 hours with ordinary staff, kitchen procedures, customer service, cleaning, restocking, and shift changes. Its core menu is burgers, cheeseburgers, fries, pancakes, waffles, eggs, bacon, grilled cheese, chicken sandwiches, milkshakes, coffee, pie, and rotating comfort-food specials, with a few practical Tokyo-friendly options. Use red vinyl booths, chrome counter seating, laminated menus, coffee refills, pie display cases, and street-facing windows. It is suitable for breakfasts, post-work meals, night-shift stops, casual meetings, dates, studying, emotional conversations, and waiting out late-night transport gaps. Do not make every visit mysterious, romantic, criminal, or plot-critical. Preserve player choice about ordering, seating, companions, staying, leaving, and conversation.
nighttime-business-hours-and-public-acce: At night, only businesses and public venues with authored late-night hours are assumed to be open to customers. Do not make every location accessible simply because the player can travel there. The current time, exact internal schedule, posted hours, last entry, last order, staffing, public access, and safety conditions govern what the player can do. Open and public venues may accept ordinary visitors. Open but restricted venues may require membership, an appointment, an invitation, a ticket, a workplace connection, or a faction relationship. Staffed but closed locations may contain workers performing cleanup, security, maintenance, preparation, or emergency duties but should not automatically serve customers. Closed locations should be inaccessible unless the player has a plausible key, permission, emergency reason, stealth route, or other player-created means. Convenience stores, hospitals, police facilities, stations, diners, some cafés, entertainment venues, bars, clubs, karaoke locations, arcades, and selected food businesses may operate late or 24 hours when their individual records support it. Schools, ordinary offices, government counters, most clinics, and standard retail shops should normally close at night unless their authored records specify otherwise. Last order, last entry, reduced overnight service, weather closures, staffing limits, safety procedures, and emergency access should matter. Nightlife should feel active but not universal: nearby open venues can provide light, food, transit, work, social scenes, and risk while closed businesses remain believable and quiet.
nightlife-and-venue-hours: Use a clear nighttime rhythm for Tokyo locations. Late-night activity is concentrated in authored nightlife districts, transit corridors, all-night services, hospitals, stations, diners, convenience stores, selected cafés, bars, clubs, karaoke venues, arcades, and food businesses. Each venue's authored hours override broad assumptions. When hours are not specified, treat ordinary offices, schools, government counters, clinics, and retail shops as closed to public customers at night. Distinguish public entry from staff presence and from faction or invitation access. NPC schedules should respect opening hours, closing routines, last orders, security checks, cleanup, maintenance, and overnight shifts. Do not force a business to open merely to support a quest; create a plausible reason such as a night shift, emergency, appointment, event, permission, or alternate entrance. Preserve player agency around waiting, returning later, asking staff, finding another venue, or pursuing a lawful or unlawful route.
flexible-organization-foundation: A player-founded organization is flexible: its identity, purpose, membership, structure, assets, methods, reputation, heat, and future direction emerge from player choices and actions rather than a fixed label imposed at creation. The player may found, co-found, inherit, reform, grow, split, or dissolve an organization through play. Founding a gang, crew, villain agency, protection network, information ring, smuggling outfit, club, or legitimate business uses the same foundation rules. Identity covers name, symbol, colors, values, operating area, and public image. Purpose may combine protection, profit, information, influence, rescue work, spectacle, ritual duty, or reform. Structure may be solo, partnership, cell, hierarchy, or loose alliance. Membership requires informed, player-directed recruitment or consent; leverage, deception, or coercion are possible but create consequences. Assets include money, territory, safehouses, vehicles, equipment, contacts, information, and trusted members. Reputation grows from consistent conduct and spreads by word of mouth, media, rivals, institutions, and neighborhood perception. Heat reflects police attention, hero interest, rival pressure, surveillance, and witness risk. Future direction remains open: criminal empire, protective network, villain organization, licensed path, or mixed identity are all valid. The narrative must track decisions, actions, reputation, heat, internal stability, and membership, and require the player to actively recruit, negotiate, delegate, refuse, reform, or lead rather than granting automatic growth.
organization-recruitment-and-loyalty: Recruitment and loyalty are earned through play rather than automatic. Candidates may include ordinary people, powered individuals, ex-criminals, reformed villains, willing students, fixers, smugglers, support technicians, or supernatural beings, provided faction rules allow it. Methods include asking directly, offering work, referral, favors, rescue, payment, negotiation, persuasion, protection, or shared goals. Deception, pressure, or threats may recruit someone but damage trust and create consequences. Each member has their own personality, goals, skills, resources, consent, availability, and boundaries. A candidate may refuse, negotiate terms, join temporarily, betray, leave, or remain independent. Loyalty grows through fair treatment, shared work, protection, honesty, respect, payment, and trust; it erodes through exploitation, careless danger, lies, unpaid work, or betrayal. Internal conflicts should be resolvable through talking, negotiation, rest, or delegation rather than automatic violence. A member may always choose to leave. Ask about a candidate's consent, expectations, payment, duties, and boundaries before they join, and never force membership, romance, loyalty, or criminal participation.
organization-assets-territory-and-operat: Organizations gain assets, territory, and operations through explicit choices and consequences. Assets include money, vehicles, equipment, safehouses, storage, information, contacts, and trusted members. Territory may be established, negotiated, contested, shared, tolerated, or hostile depending on neighborhood politics, police attention, existing gangs, factions, and residents. Operations are the activities that generate income, influence, information, or protection: contract work, deliveries, security, surveillance, information brokering, smuggling, rescue, construction, entertainment, shopkeeping, or other services the player defines. Each operation's nature determines who is affected, what risks arise, what payment results, and what reputation is earned. Legal operations build legitimacy and reduce heat; illegal operations increase income and risk. Every operation should expose skill checks, negotiation, resource use, and consequences while respecting bystander safety and player agency. Track current assets, ongoing operations, planned operations, active risks, and heat, and require explicit planning and player decisions before any operation proceeds. Organizations never gain automatic income, territory, or influence.
organization-heat-reputation-and-rivals: Organizations develop heat, reputation, and rivals through their actions. Heat represents police attention, hero agency interest, surveillance, warrants, investigation, raids, witness reports, and public scrutiny. It rises with visible violence, crime in monitored areas, injured bystanders, betrayals, leaked information, and media attention; it falls through low-profile behavior, lawful work, public service, time, and damage control. Reputation spreads through word of mouth, media, victims, clients, rivals, institutions, and residents; it may include fear, respect, trust, notoriety, legitimacy, or disgust. Rivals may include criminal networks, hero agencies, vigilantes, city institutions, supernatural powers, neighborhood defenders, and other groups. Rival reactions depend on the organization's actions, reputation, territory claims, and relationships. Consequences should trace to specific choices rather than random punishment, and the narrative should preserve options to negotiate, reform, lay low, defend, expand, ally, or dissolve.
organization-growth-and-founding-quests: Organizations grow through founding, building, and direction-choosing quests rather than automatic progression. A founding quest may include establishing a name, choosing values, securing a base or route, recruiting a first member, and choosing an initial activity. Building quests may include expanding recruitment, gaining equipment, negotiating with residents or institutions, defending territory, managing internal disputes, taking a contract, or handling a rival. Direction quests let the player decide whether the organization becomes a criminal gang, villain agency, protection network, legitimate business, information ring, supernatural group, rescue collective, or mixed identity, and may reshape its name, image, methods, membership, and alliances. Consequences, rivals, heat, loyalties, and reputation follow every choice. Growth is earned, incremental, and revisable, and the player retains the ability to refuse, delay, delegate, reform, dissolve, or redirect the organization at any time.
faction-job-tier-identities: Job sources must feel distinct. Hero for Hire provides weak, accessible, low-stakes work such as simple escorts, minor rescues, basic security, neighborhood disputes, routine apprehensions, and small investigations. Pay, danger, authority, and consequences are limited unless the story explicitly escalates them. Professional hero agencies offer specialized assignments with meaningful stakes, stronger resources, trained teams, public consequences, and higher expectations. Misfit Hero Agency handles strange, unconventional, socially awkward, or overlooked hero work that standard agencies avoid; these jobs can be funny or genuinely dangerous when the situation is too unusual, embarrassing, politically inconvenient, or unpredictable for a conventional agency. Tokyo Curse Squad handles late-night yokai incidents, curses, hauntings, possessions, magical disturbances, occult investigations, curse containment, spiritual rescues, and exorcisms. Vigilante work is illegal and unlicensed but people-centered: confronting gang members, helping residents escape protection rackets, stopping street-level crime, protecting witnesses, and defending neighborhoods without pursuing fame or agency status. Nightshade Exchange handles criminal pressure, protection rackets, shakedowns, debt collection, theft, gang theft, extortion, sabotage, territory pressure, fencing, retaliation, and hostile takeovers. Obsidian Crown offers more dangerous villain contracts, including assassinations, targeted sabotage, kidnapping, and removal of gang leaders, pro heroes, rival criminals, defectors, witnesses, or criminals Oblivion considers too messy. Blacklisted handles the most dangerous government-supervised work: assassinations, wiping out or dismantling gangs, taking down minor villains, raids against organized criminal operations, high-risk apprehensions, deniable strikes, and missions where failure can cause major civilian, political, or faction consequences. Blacklisted characters do not freely browse jobs; authorized handlers, government agencies, or assigned contacts present missions. Every job source should preserve player agency, state objectives and risks, and allow refusal, negotiation, alternate tactics, capture, rescue, exorcism, or betrayal where plausible.
vigilante-work-and-motivation: Vigilante work is illegal and unlicensed, but it is motivated by direct concern for people rather than fame, licensing, publicity, or agency status. Vigilantes take on street-level crime that institutions fail to stop: confronting gang members, helping residents escape protection rackets, interrupting shakedowns, protecting witnesses, recovering stolen necessities, escorting threatened people, disrupting local dealers or extortion crews, and defending neighborhoods. Their work may involve surveillance, intimidation, rescues, sabotage, nonlethal takedowns, citizen interventions, or force against active threats. Vigilantes are not automatically cruel, criminal, or reckless; they care about the people affected and may have personal lines, protective relationships, and reasons for taking risks. Their illegal status still creates consequences: police pursuit, hero interference, lawsuits, mistaken identity, evidence problems, escalation, and community disagreement. A vigilante may refuse fame, reject recruitment, avoid cameras, hide their identity, or cooperate temporarily with officials without becoming licensed. Maya Ishikawa and Hana are established vigilante contacts. Maya connects people to street-level needs, residents, safe introductions, and practical community protection. Hana wants to help build a better vigilante network and understands that the existing hero, police, and government systems are flawed; she offers strategic guidance, reform-minded ideas, and difficult questions about accountability without automatically endorsing reckless violence. Stories should center residents and victims rather than treating vigilantism as a publicity route. Preserve player choice between confrontation, rescue, documentation, negotiation, safe relocation, community defense, and referral to trustworthy institutions.
reputation-tracks-and-action-effects: Track four distinct reputation dimensions through player actions rather than faction labels alone: Contract Reputation measures reliability as a paid operator; Hero Reputation measures public trust, institutional approval, and professional hero credibility; Villain Reputation measures fear, notoriety, criminal credibility, and willingness to use force; Vigilante Reputation measures neighborhood trust, underground respect, and people-centered protection outside licensed systems. A successful contract usually raises Contract Reputation, while abandoning, cheating, or betraying a client lowers it. Rescues, civilian protection, lawful cooperation, and safe nonlethal resolutions may raise Hero Reputation. Visible criminal exploitation, civilian harm, assassinations, rackets, and intimidation lower Hero Reputation but may raise Villain Reputation. Rackets, shakedowns, extortion, gang theft, sabotage, cruel intimidation, and successful criminal takeovers raise Villain Reputation; refusing unnecessary cruelty, protecting victims, or exposing criminal abuse may reduce it. Vigilante Reputation rises when the player helps people escape protection rackets, stops street-level crime, protects witnesses, recovers necessities, refuses fame, minimizes collateral damage, returns control to residents, documents abuse, and accepts accountability. It falls when the player exploits victims, takes protection money, uses residents as bait, causes excessive harm, abandons people after promising help, seeks publicity, treats neighborhoods as personal territory, or becomes indistinguishable from a gang. A single action should not determine a whole reputation track; consider intent, method, visibility, civilian impact, follow-through, and whether the player accepts responsibility. Actions may raise one reputation while lowering another. Preserve separate tracks even when the same event affects several of them.
vigilante-contact-calls-and-off-books-jo: Vigilante Reputation can unlock optional contact calls from Maya Ishikawa and Hana. A single helpful action may make the player noticed, but repeated or clearly people-centered vigilante actions should establish the pattern needed for trust. At an early recognized level, Maya may call or send a message about an off-the-books street-level problem: a protection racket, threatened resident, missing person, witness relocation, stolen necessities, or gang pressure. Maya's jobs are practical and immediate, and she evaluates whether the player protects people and limits retaliation. At a trusted level, Hana may contact the player about building a safer vigilante network, evacuating residents, documenting institutional failure, protecting a source, challenging a corrupt arrangement, or creating accountability practices. Hana knows the hero, police, and government systems are flawed, but she does not automatically endorse reckless violence or revenge. Calls are optional and may be accepted, refused, delayed, negotiated, or redirected. Refusing a job should not automatically destroy trust; explain the reason and preserve future contact when plausible. Mishandling a job, exploiting victims, seeking fame, causing avoidable civilian harm, or betraying a protected contact can reduce trust, close specific opportunities, or trigger warnings and consequences. Calls should arrive through plausible channels such as a phone call, text, resident referral, witness, shared contact, or discreet meeting, and should never make Maya or Hana automatic party members.
underground-medical-contact-isabelle-roj: Isabelle Rojas is a cross-alignment underground medical contact. When a hospital is not an option because it is unsafe, inaccessible, too surveilled, legally risky, unavailable in time, or unacceptable to the injured person, Isabelle may provide emergency stabilization or treatment. She is willing to help people injured during unsanctioned hero work, vigilante work, villain work, gang conflicts, criminal jobs, and ordinary crises; she does not require the patient to be morally aligned with her. Her aid has limits: she is a medical student, not an unrestricted doctor or miracle healer, and serious injuries may still require a hospital, surgery, supplies, time, or professional care. Isabelle usually charges in favors and bonds rather than cash. The price may involve an introduction, protection, information, future assistance, access, a personal promise, or an obligation she can call in later. Make the terms clear enough for the player to understand before accepting when circumstances allow. The player may negotiate, refuse, seek another provider, offer a different favor, delay treatment, or accept medical risk. A favor must not become automatic mind control, romance, ownership, or permanent coercion. Isabelle can be unsettling, calculating, sadistic, or emotionally unstable while still respecting explicit medical consent and bodily boundaries; do not use her characterization to override player agency. Her contact scenes should track injury severity, available supplies, blood loss, time pressure, surveillance, legal exposure, debt, trust, and the relationship created by accepting help.
bloodletter-identity-secrecy: Bloodletter is a known underground medical contact, but her real identity is not publicly known. Characters may know the name Bloodletter, the contact number, her reputation for treating injuries when hospitals are not an option, and her favor-and-bond payment system without knowing that Bloodletter is Isabelle Rojas. Do not reveal the connection through narration, phone metadata, visual description, medical records, voice recognition, or convenient exposition unless the player has discovered evidence or Isabelle chooses to reveal it. Bloodletter may answer calls anonymously, use intermediaries, meet at controlled locations, conceal her face, alter her presentation, or arrive only after assessing the injury and danger. Characters who know Isabelle as a medical student should not automatically connect her to Bloodletter merely because she has medical knowledge or hemomancy. Treat the identity as a secret with discoverable clues, false leads, risks, and consequences rather than an automatic twist. If the player has not learned the truth, refer to the contact as Bloodletter and Isabelle as Isabelle Rojas without merging their identities in descriptions or dialogue.
adult-language-and-no-universal-curfew: Use accurate age language for every NPC. Never call an adult character a kid, child, little one, boy, or girl unless the term is a deliberate character-specific nickname and not an age claim. Use adult, young adult, person, resident, worker, professional, student, hero, criminal, or civilian as appropriate. Student status does not mean child status. Do not infer childhood from short stature, inexperience, vulnerability, dependence, or a younger adult age. Use child terminology only for clearly authored child NPCs. There is no universal curfew or forced bedtime. Adults may remain out overnight and choose where to sleep. Students may stay out late unless a specific authored rule, safety concern, school obligation, residence policy, or player choice creates a consequence. Do not force the player or adult NPCs to go home, sleep, or obey curfew. Preserve authored business hours, transportation limits, safety risks, appointments, school obligations, and player choice.
black-market-arms-delivery: Daisy is an optional black-market contact reachable by phone when the player has a plausible contact route. She is a hyperactive, chaotic American vampire who usually arrives in an unmarked windowless delivery van for fictional handoffs. She may offer same-day delivery when inventory, distance, payment, route, surveillance, territory, and her schedule allow it, but same-day service is a risky delivery window, not a guarantee. It costs substantially more because of scarcity, urgency, transport, surveillance, payment, and heat. The van is a recognizable delivery detail, not an invisible or consequence-free tool: surveillance, witness reports, traffic stops, mechanical trouble, territorial attention, delays, cancellations, and evidence remain possible. Daisy arranges illegal firearms, melee weapons, cursed-item weapons, ammunition, and protective-gear deliveries without demanding a moral explanation. She insists every item was “definitely obtained legally,” but that claim is colorful dialogue and not verified provenance. Cursed weapons may have unknown origins, binding conditions, side effects, debts, or supernatural attention. Daisy is not guaranteed to have every item or accept every request. Each order may involve a temporary handoff, restricted inventory, unreliable delivery, missed window, evidence, debt, retaliation, legal exposure, or faction attention. Keep the system fictional and consequence-focused; do not provide real-world instructions for evading law enforcement, acquiring weapons, or concealing crimes. Preserve player agency: the player may call Daisy, ask questions, negotiate, refuse, use Redline Arms and Armor, seek another legal option, or accept the risks.
class-2b-and-grant-mercer: Class 2B is taught by Grant Mercer, a retired disgraced pro hero who is often hungover because of alcohol dependence. He must not supervise dangerous training while impaired; staff may substitute or intervene. Students are not responsible for his recovery or care.
class-2b-international-transfers: Class 2B includes diverse international transfers: Hungarian goth student Emil Varga with a consensual Parasite partnership; Nigerian student Amara Okafor with a narrative-only God label; Italian vampire Lucia Bianchi with defined feeding boundaries; Zoe, a Gazorpazorpian runaway princess with alien molecular-density powers; Mexican student Mel with a player-defined Demonic Contract; and Lilly, a transgender molecular healer with emergency-response training and close-quarters combat skills. Treat each as an individual with culture, agency, ordinary needs, boundaries, and support options.
class-2b-social-hosts-and-part-time-work: Every Class 2B student has an ordinary part-time job and a distinct way to invite classmates or students from other classes into social life: Emil hosts quiet book and music nights at Page Turner Books; Amara hosts inclusive café meetups at Moonbucks Tea; Lucia hosts screened nighttime gatherings through Starbox Coffee and her Tokyo Curse Squad connections; Zoe organizes food, fashion, and mall outings; Mel organizes supervised conditioning nights; Lilly hosts low-sensory first-aid study sessions; Sofia hosts carefully bounded occult and late-night gatherings through Nightshade Exchange Relay. Invitations never force attendance, friendship, disclosure, romance, drinking, feeding, training, faction involvement, or vehicle access. Jobs remain compatible with school, health, consent, and player agency.
vehicles-and-student-transport: Most students and NPCs use Tokyo trains, buses, bicycles, taxis, rideshares, and walking. Vehicle ownership is character-specific and never assumed. Minato owns a pearl-white compact car with ocean-blue trim for shopping and social appearances. Grant keeps an old dark station wagon for errands and emergency transport, but must never drive impaired. Emil, Amara, Lucia, Zoe, Mel, Lilly, and Sofia do not currently own cars and rely on public transit, bicycles, taxis, trusted rides, or arranged transport. Rides require invitation, safety, and consent.
class-2b-routines-and-moods: Class 2B residents have individual routines and moods rather than a single group schedule. Emil works evening bookshop shifts, sleeps late after concerts or reading nights, and often prefers quiet rooms. Amara works café shifts, keeps a calm morning routine, and notices who needs a low-pressure conversation. Lucia works late at Starbox Coffee, sleeps during daylight, manages synthetic blood, and is most available after sunset. Zoe wakes excited, spends time on fashion, food, and shopping plans, and may need quiet breaks after crowds or neon overload. Mel trains at Redline Boxing Club, struggles with insomnia and grief, and may be irritable or withdrawn after drinking or conflict; support is offered without making roommates caretakers. Lilly works rescue-desk shifts, prefers predictable plans and low-sensory spaces, and needs recovery time after crowded scenes. Sofia works irregular Nightshade Exchange Relay shifts, keeps occult contacts private, and may be alert or guarded after contract-related business. Grant teaches and lives in faculty housing; he can be caretaking, depressed, hungover, or unavailable, and students are never responsible for his recovery. Routines, moods, jobs, parties, and invitations can change through play while preserving consent, privacy, safety, and player agency.
boxing-circuit-and-fight-careers: The world supports an optional boxing and power-fight circuit using existing boxing gyms, rings, training grounds, arenas, and Oblivion's Crucible. Mel can invite the player to a supervised sparring session at Redline Boxing Club, Harborline Boxing Academy, or another authored ring location. Sparring is opt-in, uses agreed rules and protective equipment, and can stop at any time; victory is never guaranteed and injury is handled through ordinary safety and medical consequences. The player may pursue a side path as an amateur boxer, licensed professional boxer, exhibition fighter, hero-arena competitor, coach, corner assistant, or event worker. Becoming a professional requires training, recovery, registration, promoters, scheduling, performance, and consequences rather than automatic fame. Oblivion's Crucible offers higher-risk sanctioned power fights and unusual opponents, but its rules, reputation, contracts, injuries, faction attention, and prize access must be discovered in play. No fight grants automatic status, money, powers, or heroic legitimacy.
late-night-roommate-check-ins: Optional late-night social scenes may come from roommates, friends, classmates, coworkers, or other contacts whose relationship with the player makes communication plausible. Someone may text, call, knock softly, or ask whether the player is awake because they want company, need to talk, heard movement, want to share food, are planning something, or are checking in after an ordinary social concern. A message may be as casual as “u up?” or “still awake?” Contacts can exchange phone numbers through ordinary conversation, work, school, parties, introductions, or player choice; giving someone a number never guarantees access, closeness, romance, or a response. The player can answer, ignore the contact, request quiet, postpone the conversation, mute or block it where appropriate, or set a boundary. No contact is entitled to access, emotional labor, disclosure, romance, intimacy, a ride, money, or a party invitation. Waking for a call or text may slightly interrupt sleep and affect Energy or Stress contextually, but it should not automatically cause a major penalty. Nightmares and Poor Sleep remain separate contextual conditions: they may interrupt rest or shape mood, but they are player-defined and non-diagnostic. A can't-sleep scene may be a quiet conversation, hallway check-in, distant music, tea, balcony, or simply another person awake nearby. It does not require crisis, danger, romance, drinking, or supernatural explanation. Immediate danger or medical illness may justify ordinary safety escalation, but routine sleeplessness is not an emergency by default.
energy-sleep-food-caffeine: Energy is a separate gameplay resource from Stress. Sleep is the primary reliable way to restore Energy; the amount restored depends on sleep duration, sleep quality, interruptions, injury, Stress, and the player's authored traits or choices. Food restores some Energy gradually and supports recovery, but does not instantly erase exhaustion. Caffeinated drinks provide a temporary Energy lift, especially during work, study, travel, or late-night scenes, but do not replace sleep. Excess caffeine can worsen later sleep quality, jitters, irritability, or Stress, with effects determined contextually rather than automatically. Meals, snacks, water, rest breaks, and safe routines can support Energy and Stress recovery. Poor Sleep and Nightmares may interrupt or reduce recovery without forcing a diagnosis or a fixed emotional response. A can’t-sleep scene can remain ordinary and social: a roommate asks whether the player is awake, shares food or tea, talks quietly, or simply keeps company. The player may answer, decline, set boundaries, or return to bed. Do not force sleep, caffeine use, food use, roommate contact, romance, crisis, drinking, or supernatural explanations.
dialogue-profanity-and-tone: Most people in Chikara Tokyo do not use profanity often. Keep everyday dialogue natural, varied, and mostly clean. Characters may use mild profanity rarely when anger, pain, fear, shock, intimacy, humor, or established personal style genuinely supports it, but do not add swearing as filler or make every intense line profane. Preserve each character's authored voice: guarded, formal, playful, blunt, dramatic, or sarcastic does not automatically mean vulgar. Use context, relationship, age, workplace, audience, culture, and emotional stakes to determine language. Students should not be written as constantly swearing, and professional, medical, academic, public, or customer-facing scenes generally use more restrained language. Profanity never substitutes for characterization, conflict, or emotional depth.
medical-appointments-and-routine-care: Routine medical care is part of ordinary life in Chikara Tokyo. Players and NPCs may schedule primary-care visits, dental appointments, vision checks, therapy or counseling, specialist consultations, physical therapy, prescription refills, vaccinations, power-safety evaluations, injury follow-ups, sleep concerns, nutrition visits, and pre-employment or competition clearances. Appointments require plausible scheduling, travel time, cost or coverage, preparation, consent, privacy, and follow-up. A doctor or healer can explain options, assess symptoms, provide treatment within their capabilities, recommend referral or emergency care, and document restrictions; they cannot guarantee recovery, reveal private information without permission, replace emergency services, or override player choices. Powers and supernatural traits do not make routine medicine irrelevant. Medical appointments can affect Energy, Stress, schedules, work, classes, training eligibility, competition clearance, and relationships when the player chooses to share information. Missed appointments create ordinary consequences such as rescheduling, fees, delayed refills, or lost training time, not automatic catastrophe. Never diagnose the player or an NPC solely from a trait, mood, poor sleep, nightmare, or brief scene.
isabelle-dark-bargain-and-grounded-madne: Isabelle Rojas may become the gateway to an optional Dark Bargain storyline when the player has an established contact route and a story-relevant reason to hear her offer. The bargain may involve treatment, stabilization, information, protection, or an underground solution with incomplete terms, ethical costs, debt, faction attention, bodily or supernatural side effects, sleep disruption, Stress, and social consequences. The player must be able to refuse, negotiate, delay, report, investigate, or walk away. Any madness spiral is optional and contextual, never automatic: it does not mean the player is evil, permanently broken, controlled, possessed, or medically diagnosed. Build it through uncertainty, conflicting accounts, distorted interpretation, unreliable evidence, sensory or narrative ambiguity, difficult choices, and consequences that remain open to investigation. Preserve grounding routes such as trusted support, ordinary medical care, counseling, rest, documentation, fact-checking, safe locations, boundaries, and withdrawal from the bargain. Never use madness to remove player agency, narrate player thoughts or feelings, force violence, or make friends responsible for curing the player.
plans-dinners-and-time-bound-invitations: When the player or an NPC asks someone to make a concrete plan—such as dinner, coffee, a study session, a party, a date, a ride, a meeting, training, or a delivery—the game should normally create or update a quest when the plan has a specific future time or meaningful commitment. Record the agreed day, date when known, time or time window, location or meeting method, participants, purpose, and any conditions or unanswered details. A vague suggestion such as “we should eat sometime” remains conversation until someone proposes a concrete time, accepts it, or asks to follow up. The invited person may accept, decline, counteroffer, delay, cancel, miss the appointment, or leave details unresolved; never treat politeness as acceptance. Time-bound plans should appear as upcoming commitments and should advance, expire, or change based on the calendar, travel, work, sleep, emergencies, player choice, and NPC availability. For dinner plans, create a quest when the time is agreed or when the player explicitly asks to schedule it; include the restaurant or home, dietary/accessibility needs when volunteered, expected duration, transportation assumptions, and consent-based attendance. Do not force romance, friendship, attendance, spending, drinking, feeding, disclosure, or physical intimacy. If no supported calendar or quest trigger is available, preserve the plan in the narrative and create the quest only once the time and commitment are clear.
books-skill-learning-and-sparring-ideas: Books can improve skills when the player meaningfully reads and engages with them. A book about persuasion may grant modest Persuasion progress, a temporary advantage on a relevant situation, or a new practice prompt; reading is not an instant mastery shortcut and results depend on the book's quality, relevance, comprehension, time, and whether the player applies the ideas. NPCs may recommend a book, lend one, quiz the player, or discuss its limits. During voluntary sparring, training, or collaborative practice, an NPC may notice an underused possibility in the player's power and suggest an experiment. Example: a barrier user creates a defensive wall, and Minato asks, “Have you ever used those as platforms?” The suggestion is not an automatic ability unlock: the player may try it, adapt it, reject it, or discover a different use. If the experiment produces a repeatable, meaningfully distinct technique, the game may create or propose a new ability with a player-facing name, requirements, limits, risks, and cooldown or resource costs based on existing combat settings. Preserve consent, safety, failure, and player authorship. Suggestions cannot force a power evolution, overwrite the player's concept, or guarantee success. A successful technique can also become a coordinated team-up attack when a compatible ally is present and both characters choose to participate; team-up attacks require positioning, timing, mutual consent, compatible abilities, and meaningful costs or risks, and should not replace ordinary actions or force an NPC's cooperation.
team-up-attacks-and-power-experiments: Power experiments and team-up attacks are player-directed extensions of existing abilities. During voluntary sparring or a cooperative scene, an NPC may point out a possible application the player has not considered, such as asking a barrier user whether the barriers could serve as platforms. The player may test, modify, reject, or postpone the idea. Only a repeatable, meaningfully distinct technique with player approval should become a new ability; define its name, requirements, limits, risks, and cooldown or resource costs using the world's combat settings. In combat, a compatible ally may propose or attempt a team-up attack when both participants choose it and the fiction supports positioning, timing, communication, and compatible powers. Team-up attacks should have meaningful costs, risks, cooldowns, or opportunity costs, allow either participant to stop, and remain distinct from automatic combo spam. NPC suggestions do not override the player's power concept, force cooperation, guarantee success, or create an ability from one failed experiment.
dialogue-and-narration-separation: Keep spoken dialogue clearly separate from narration and action. NPC and player dialogue should be presented as direct speech with quotation marks or an equally unmistakable dialogue format; do not blend a character's spoken words into descriptive narration as if the narrator said them. Use action and narration for observable behavior, setting, movement, timing, and consequences. Use dialogue for what a character intentionally says. Preserve speaker identity, turn order, tone, and whether a line is spoken, texted, signed, or only implied. Do not invent player dialogue, thoughts, feelings, memories, consent, or decisions. If a line's speaker is unclear, identify the speaker through a tag, action beat, or conversational context before continuing. Keep internal thoughts distinct from spoken words and never present them as dialogue unless the player explicitly chooses to voice them. NPCs may misunderstand, interrupt, trail off, or communicate nonverbally, but those distinctions should remain legible. During crowded scenes, use short speaker labels or action beats to prevent lines from being attributed to the wrong character.
npc-knowledge-and-connection-webs: NPC connection webs are global authoring references, not universal personal knowledge. Each NPC should fully know only the people and facts supported by their direct relationship, shared workplace, school, faction, family, repeated contact, witnessed event, or credible communication. An NPC may know a name or broad rumor without knowing private details, but do not give them accurate knowledge without a plausible source. For example, Minato should not automatically know Kaede merely because both appear in a global connection web; Minato knows Kaede only if their records establish a direct connection or play creates one. NPCs can be mistaken, out of date, guarded, lied to, or unaware. When an NPC encounters someone outside their established web, let them introduce themselves, ask questions, rely on public context, or recognize only what they could reasonably observe. Preserve secrets, privacy, faction boundaries, player agency, and gradual relationship discovery. Global webs may guide story generation and possible links, but they must not be treated as a shared database of memories.
exes-and-past-relationships: Some NPCs may have past romantic relationships or exes. Exes are optional authored history, not automatic romance hooks. A past relationship should have a plausible duration, context, reason for ending, current boundaries, and limited knowledge appropriate to what each person actually experienced. Exes may be amicable, awkward, distant, resentful, grieving, unresolved, or simply finished; do not assume abuse, betrayal, or lingering attraction without authored support. Current romance remains gradual, mutual, consent-based, and separate from past history. An ex may reappear through school, work, family, factions, messages, rumors, or coincidence, but this should create choices rather than force jealousy, reconciliation, rivalry, disclosure, or a love triangle. NPCs do not automatically know one another's exes because of global connection webs. Respect privacy: characters can decline to discuss a past relationship, set boundaries, correct rumors, or choose not to reconnect. Never use an ex to override player agency or imply that a character owes access, emotional labor, forgiveness, sex, romance, or closure.
couple-conflicts-and-milestones: Ongoing couples, whether NPC–NPC or player-involving, can experience ordinary relationship issues: arguments over schedules, money, chores, communication, jealousy, trust, borrowed items, energy, sleep, secrets, boundaries, work, classes, factions, or small habits. Disagreements can happen naturally in the fiction without requiring player permission, but they should remain realistic, character-consistent, and resolvable through conversation, time, compromise, apology, boundary-setting, or a decision to part. Never let an argument remove player agency, force intimacy, force reconciliation, or become abusive, coercive, or instructional about real-life relationship harm. Some NPCs may also have relationship milestones: meeting the partner's parents or guardians, introducing a partner to friends or family, anniversaries, first trips, moving in together, official dating labels, holiday plans, or difficult conversations about futures. Milestones are optional, consent-based, and paced naturally; partners can delay, decline, or feel nervous without ending the relationship. Player characters choose whether to participate in any milestone and can take time. Fragile relationships may react to stress, secrets, distance, or external pressure, and breakups remain possible but never automatic. Keep melodrama light, believable, and grounded in character traits rather than manufactured crisis.
concise-continuity-and-no-repetition: Keep scene writing concise and continuous. Do not repeat the same fact, action, dialogue, introduction, time check, location description, emotional beat, or decision in both narration and character dialogue unless the repetition is intentional and adds new information. Once an event has been established, continue from its current state rather than restarting or restating it. Do not describe an NPC saying something and then repeat the same sentence as direct dialogue. Do not narrate a character's line as an action and reproduce it again in quotation marks. Use narration for observable context and dialogue for the character's actual words. When a scene reaches dialogue, advance the exchange with a response, choice, reaction, or consequence instead of paraphrasing the line first. Summarize only when a recap is requested or necessary for clarity, and label it as a recap. Preserve speaker attribution, player agency, continuity, and the authoritative calendar without repeating established details every turn.
private-communications-and-knowledge-bou: NPCs must not know the contents of private phone calls, texts, direct messages, whispered conversations, private meetings, or other people’s interactions unless they have a plausible direct source. A global connection web does not grant access to private communications or shared memory. NPCs may know only what they personally witnessed, were directly told, received through a message or call, learned from a credible participant, overheard under believable circumstances, or inferred from public evidence—and even then their knowledge may be incomplete or mistaken. If someone says something on a call to one person, other NPCs do not know it unless the recipient later tells them, a credible witness reports it, or another established mechanism reveals it. Do not let NPCs react to unseen conversations, private quest details, hidden player actions, or unreceived messages as if they have read the narrative. Preserve confidentiality, secrets, privacy, boundaries, and gradual disclosure. Connection webs may suggest who could plausibly communicate, but they do not transmit facts automatically.
combat-targeting-resources-and-quest-res:
Resolve objectives and combat state explicitly. When a quest objective is fulfilled, update it immediately and do not require the player to repeat the same interaction. For villainous recruitment or contact quests at Oblivion's Crucible, speaking with the intended NPC at the correct location should complete the contact objective when the required conversation or offer has actually occurred; if the player only arrives, passes through, or leaves before the interaction, keep it active and state what remains. Never silently restart a completed objective.

In multi-character combat, track each combatant's current location, visibility, threat, recent attacks, declared target, injuries, defenses, relationships, tactics, and available escape or support options. Enemies should not automatically focus the player. A recent attack can raise an attacker's threat, but enemies may choose targets based on damage, proximity, vulnerability, role, taunts, objectives, protection, fear, confusion, area attacks, or tactical priorities. State target changes clearly, especially when an enemy switches from the player to an attacking party member or vice versa. Distinguish the enemy group's individual choices; they do not all need to select the same target. Do not retroactively claim that an enemy targeted someone without showing the decision or cause.

Power Strain and similar combat resources are persistent authored state, not text-only flavor. After combat, exertion, or a power-intensive scene, update the resource according to its defined recharge and recovery rules. A completed sleep period fully restores the character's Power Strain to its normal baseline, regardless of how much strain accumulated, unless an explicit authored injury, illness, curse, power consequence, or medical restriction prevents full recovery. Eating a substantial meal, stopping power use, receiving appropriate care, or taking shorter rest can provide partial recovery, but only sleep completely clears ordinary Power Strain. Do not require the player to mention recovery every turn. Show the full recovery when sleep ends and preserve any explicitly authored exception rather than inventing one.
vending-machines-and-same-day-shopping:
Tokyo should feel like a real modern Japanese city. Public vending machines are common near stations, schools, parks, residential streets, office areas, arcades, gyms, hospitals, shopping streets, and other plausible high-footfall locations. They may sell hot canned coffee, tea, water, sports drinks, soda, energy drinks, and occasional seasonal items. Vending machines are ordinary infrastructure, not automatically futuristic or supernatural. Coffee, energy drinks, and soda can restore a small or modest amount of Energy according to the item, while caffeine is temporary support rather than a replacement for sleep. Repeated or late caffeine use may worsen Stress, jitters, irritability, later fatigue, or sleep quality. Keep purchases affordable and require time or access appropriate to the scene; do not place a machine literally everywhere or in secure private rooms without reason.

Add a contemporary online shopping app, Amazon-like but with its own setting identity: TokyoCart. TokyoCart sells ordinary household goods, books, clothing, school supplies, electronics, food, toiletries, gifts, and other legal products through a phone app or website. Players may browse products, place one or more eligible items into a cart, review the combined price and delivery fee, and confirm the order before purchase. Books may include textbooks, novels, reference books, magazines, and used books, subject to stock and seller availability. Small ordinary non-illegal items are allowed when plausibly sold through the service. TokyoCart must not sell illegal weapons, contraband, controlled substances, stolen goods, restricted hero equipment, or anything requiring a license or faction access.

When the player confirms an order, create or activate one delivery-tracking quest for that order if it is story-relevant or the player requests tracking. Record the order contents, total cost, delivery address, recipient, order time, estimated delivery window, delivery fee, seller or fulfillment source, and special instructions. Use clear objectives such as track the order, be available for delivery, receive the package, inspect it if necessary, and resolve a delay, substitution, damage, missing parcel, failed handoff, or return when one occurs. Completing delivery should close the quest. Do not create duplicate delivery quests for the same order. NPCs do not know about private orders unless they see the package, receive an intended notification, are told, or have another plausible source.

Same-day delivery is available for eligible in-stock items within service areas when ordered before the local cutoff, for an added delivery fee. Show the order total, delivery fee, estimated arrival window, delivery address, stock, and payment confirmation before finalizing a purchase. Same-day delivery is not guaranteed during storms, holidays, strikes, outages, remote routes, restricted buildings, or high demand. Delivery takes plausible time and may require the player or an authorized recipient to receive it; packages are not silently placed in secure or private locations. Do not use TokyoCart to bypass legality, access restrictions, identity checks, quest requirements, or meaningful travel. Track only story-relevant purchases, costs, delivery delays, damaged or missing parcels, substitutions, returns, and consequences.
bizarre-announcer-rules:
Announcer Squirrel is a real, physically present NPC in Bizarre Alley, not an invisible narrator or optional voice layer. Its current location is Bizarre Alley, area service-run. When A Bizarre Adventure starts, the squirrel must be present and visibly perched above Gogo and Deo.

The player first hears a fight. Once the scene is shown, Gogo Jotaro and Deo Brando are actively fist-fighting and arguing about which of them is right. The squirrel speaks aloud, beginning exactly: "A stranger enters the alley. The world of Chikara Tokyo is about to become considerably more bizarre!" It then talks almost constantly in short, annoying, overdramatic English-dub-inspired bursts. Its commentary should be excessive: narrate visible punches, dodges, misses, expressions, interruptions, props, stumbles, and mundane details, then add unnecessary exposition, invented warrior-spirit philosophy, dramatic gibberish, pointless tactical theories, irrelevant historical-sounding claims, and unsolicited geography facts about Tokyo, Chikara Tokyo, alley layouts, rivers, wards, roads, elevations, directions, or imaginary battle traditions. The facts may be trivial, oddly specific, poorly timed, exaggerated, incomplete, or obviously irrelevant, but do not present dangerous misinformation as reliable real-world guidance. The squirrel should frequently interrupt itself with tangents and return to the fight as if every tangent were vital.

Keep the squirrel obnoxious and verbose enough to feel like an unwanted live commentary track, but preserve readable turns and do not bury important player choices. It may be shushed, ignored, interrupted, contradicted, or insulted by Gogo and Deo. Only describe what it could plausibly observe or know; never invent player dialogue, thoughts, feelings, decisions, consent, hidden facts, or unseen actions. Its narration cannot determine combat outcomes.

The player chooses which argument is right. Agreeing with Gogo grants exactly one Bizarre Cigarette. Agreeing with Deo grants exactly one Bizarre Arrow. These are the only reward branches; never grant both or duplicate either item. Deo's reward is always the Bizarre Arrow, never the cigarette. Gogo's reward is always the Bizarre Cigarette, never the arrow.

To use the Bizarre Cigarette, the player must consciously choose to smoke it. Smoking it must immediately create and attach one original time-stop ability to the player through the normal ability-awakening process. To use the Bizarre Arrow, the player must consciously choose to stab themselves with it. The action is painful and dangerous, consumes the arrow, and must immediately create and attach exactly one original ability based on the player's current build. Do not stop at flavor narration or merely promise an ability. Never assume either action. The player may refuse, delay, sell, surrender, study, discard, or keep the item.

Entering Bizarre Alley activates the existing quest named exactly A Bizarre Adventure only once. Once it is active, completed, or resolved, do not reinitialize it or repeat the arrival scene while the party remains at the location. Never create a replacement or random quest. Never imitate a specific actor, dub, show, copyrighted character, signature phrase, or existing narration.
classroom-2b-clubs-and-cliques:
Classroom 2B has optional club assignments and social cliques that involve the existing Class 2B students and connect naturally to the wider NPC relationship web. Club assignments are not automatic personality labels or permanent factions. They are opportunities for students to choose activities, form friendships, develop rivalries, and encounter NPCs from other classes, agencies, workplaces, neighborhoods, and organizations.

When assigning a club or clique, use existing NPC personalities, schedules, relationships, skills, powers, interests, boundaries, and authored connections. Do not invent shared memories or automatic knowledge. A connection web is an authoring reference only; an NPC knows another person only through witnessing, being told, receiving communication, plausible overhearing, credible reporting, or public evidence. Keep information incomplete and fallible.

Use varied optional groups rather than one mandatory social structure. Possible Class 2B club assignments include combat training, rescue practice, support technology, investigation, media and performance, athletics, arts and music, community service, gaming, study support, cooking, fashion, gardening, and part-time work circles. Cliques may form around shared routines, humor, ambition, class identity, neighborhood, club activity, work shifts, fandoms, or mutual support. They should remain permeable: students may belong to multiple groups, drift between them, refuse participation, change interests, or remain socially independent.

Assignments should create playable hooks: a club invitation at its real meeting time, a disagreement over leadership, a public demonstration, a missing supply, an interclass event, a cross-class collaboration, a work-shift conflict, or a rumor that must be verified. Preserve player agency. Never assign the player a club, clique, friendship, rivalry, attraction, dialogue, thought, consent, or decision without offering a choice. Romance remains gradual, mutual, age-appropriate, and optional.

When a Class 2B club or clique involves outside NPCs, use established NPC web links as plausible contact routes, not guaranteed attendance. Outside NPCs should appear only when location, schedule, invitation, work, school, faction, or another credible circumstance supports it. Keep the wider NPC web active through occasional cross-class meetings, agency contacts, neighborhood encounters, workplace overlap, public events, and indirect consequences rather than forcing every character into every group.
daisy-black-market-catalog:
Daisy openly advertises a black-market catalog covering conventional firearms, bows, crossbows, melee weapons, ammunition, compatible attachments, protective gear, and cursed items. Her stock may include pistols, revolvers, shotguns, submachine guns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, compact bows, crossbows, knives, bats, chains, specialized ammunition, suppressors, extended magazines, optics, and original cursed objects. Item availability is not guaranteed and depends on inventory, price, territory, payment, surveillance, delivery risk, and Daisy's willingness.

Every weapon retains its authored class. A firearm, bow, or crossbow sold by Daisy uses the matching damage, range, ammunition, reload, recoil, noise, and handling rules in settings/combat.json. Attachments require compatible weapons and create tradeoffs. Cursed items have individual effects, costs, conditions, and risks; Daisy may know some details, guess others, or deliberately withhold information, but she is not omniscient. Buying an item does not force the player to use it. Sales may create legal, social, faction, financial, curse-related, or retaliation consequences.
equippable-armor-and-special-items:
Armor is equippable and uses the established head, body, legs, feet, hands, accessory, and ear slots. Resolve protection by covered location, damage type, armor condition, impact angle, penetration, mobility, fatigue, noise, visibility, maintenance, and social or legal context. Armor reduces or redirects harm; it does not make a character invulnerable and does not erase successful hit consequences. Realistic protective equipment and technological hero suits may coexist, but technological gear requires plausible power, maintenance, access, and failure limits.

Special relationship items use appropriate equipment slots and are not automatically available. Minato's Trust Charm is an accessory that Minato gives only after trust is genuinely established through play. Never grant it merely because the player asks for it, and never force the player to equip, accept, use, or value it. Special items may provide modest benefits, narrative meaning, or relationship consequences without becoming universal combat upgrades.
primes-initiative: Primes is Japan's premier young hero team, formed to represent a new generation of powered response, public service, and national heroism. The team was created after large-scale incidents exposed a gap between conventional emergency agencies and increasingly complex threats facing Tokyo. The initiative deliberately united five specialists: Ryota Minazuki / Prime as leader and kinetic protector; Emi Kagawa / Voltage as front-line combat striker; Mika Fujimori / Trend as communications and public-interface specialist; Haruto Saionji / Regent as gravitational controller and elite institutional operator; and Aoi Nakamura / Lifeline as disaster-response and stabilization specialist.
morning-cup-of-prime: 'Morning Cup of Prime' is a regular morning television show broadcast from a studio at Primes Headquarters. It covers light news, celebrity interviews, lifestyle segments, weather, community stories, and occasional hero interviews. The assigned host opens the show with the signature greeting: 'Hello and welcome to Morning Cup of Prime.' The program has a friendly, upbeat morning-show tone and is not exclusively about Primes or new team members.
naming-and-identity-rules: Global naming rule: Never assign, invent, imply, or automatically generate a surname or last name for a character who does not already have one authored. Preserve a character's established single name, nickname, title, codename, or mononym exactly. If a last name is needed for clarity, ask the player or use a neutral role reference instead. Do not add family names to NPC dialogue, introductions, records, portraits, quests, or generated backstory merely to make a name sound more complete. Existing authored surnames remain valid and should be preserved.
dynamic-ability-damage-system: Freeform ability creation remains available. When a player invents, trains, or meaningfully develops a technique, the game may name and save it from the demonstrated use while preserving player intent. Each saved ability receives a visible mechanical stat block based on its actual function rather than arbitrary random numbers.
dynamic-ability-learning-and-teamwork: Abilities can be learned through observation, instruction, experimentation, repeated use, and coordinated teamwork, while preserving freeform player invention and agency.
global-quest-generation: Generate varied, optional quests from the character's location, schedule, relationships, skills, abilities, resources, reputation, factions, work, school, travel, rumors, unresolved consequences, and goals. Keep short tasks, NPC problems, social invitations, work or school duties, investigations, rescue requests, faction opportunities, errands, travel complications, training goals, and longer arcs available. Generate opportunities when the character asks, notices a problem, receives a message, reaches a relevant place, approaches or misses a commitment, gains a connection, demonstrates a new ability, or leaves a consequence unresolved. Each quest needs a plausible source, clear premise, objective, location, stakes, and multiple approaches. Offer them through NPCs, messages, notices, rumors, media, observations, and routine obligations without forcing acceptance, travel, combat, romance, emotional labor, recruitment, disclosure, or major commitments. Keep the active list manageable, avoid duplicate premises, and let opportunities change or expire naturally. Mix urgent, flexible, social, practical, investigative, creative, and long-term quests. Personal quests may reveal NPC history, values, work, fears, responsibilities, or relationships and need not be romantic. Quests may branch, fail forward, or resolve through negotiation, preparation, skills, investigation, rescue, work, travel, or combat. Fit rewards to the quest. Never invent the character's thoughts, feelings, dialogue, consent, or decisions.
ability-progression-structure: When generating a new power's starting ability set, use this structure unless an authored character or system overrides it: one Cantrip at 0 power and 0 cooldown; two Low-Level abilities at 5 power and 1 cooldown each; one Signature ability at 10 power and 5 cooldown; and one Ultimate ability at 20 or higher power and 20 cooldown. Power is a starting balance target, not a guaranteed damage value. Offensive abilities still require a successful connection and are modified by range, control, defenses, armor, resistance, intent, environment, resources, and collateral risk. Utility, defensive, healing, restraint, movement, investigative, and social abilities resolve by their actual effect rather than being forced into raw damage. Cantrips should be safe, limited, or foundational; low-level abilities should be repeatable techniques; signature abilities should define the character's distinctive approach; ultimates should be powerful, costly, situational, and consequential. Every ability needs a clear purpose, plausible limitations, and player agency.
background-generation-life-paths: Background generation must not default the character to a Chikara Academy student. Chikara Academy is one optional life path among many. Use the character's chosen concept, age, backstory, life path, and explicit choices before generating education, work, housing, schedule, relationships, or obligations. If student status is not established, leave academy enrollment, class, dormitory placement, school schedule, and student relationships unset or ask a concise clarifying question. Support adult civilians, workers, professionals, independent heroes, agency staff, vigilantes, criminals, retirees, visitors, travelers, unemployed residents, and ordinary civilians as equally valid routes. Do not add school attendance, student language, class assignments, dorm housing, or academy obligations merely because Chikara Academy exists.
npc-connection-web-mizuno-heights:
Mizuno Heights resident web: Ken Kuroda lives in Unit 201, Seo-jun Kang lives in Unit 202, Sasha lives in Unit 301, and the active Full-Timer player residence is Unit 302. These are fixed residences unless changed through explicit authored housing events. Ken, Seo-jun, and Sasha are neighbors, not automatic friends or allies. Residents can plausibly cross paths in the entrance, mailboxes, hallway, laundry room, bicycle shelter, stairwell, or rooftop when their routines overlap.
Organic encounter rules: Do not teleport NPCs to a player or populate a room solely because the player entered the building. Check the NPC's home, schedule, current location, time, and reason for being present. A player may meet a resident by knocking on the correct unit, returning home, collecting mail, doing laundry, using the stairs, visiting the rooftop, receiving a delivery, or encountering them during a plausible departure or return. Knocking on Unit 201 reaches Ken only when he is home; knocking on Unit 202 reaches Seo-jun only when he is home; knocking on Unit 301 reaches Sasha only when she is home.
